title: Measuring R&D Automation: RE-Bench, PaperBench, MLE-bench, Time Horizons

questions.question: Which set of components does an operational 'automating AI R&D' claim need before it can be compared with another such claim?
options: A model name, a release date, a parameter count and a training-compute figure
A task distribution, a human baseline, a success criterion and a budget
A benchmark leaderboard, a company press release, a demo video and a blog post
A context-window length, a tokens-per-second rate, a price and an uptime figure
questions.explanation: Without all four, 'intern-level' has no content: RE-Bench shows the budget alone flips the verdict between agents and humans.

questions.question: On RE-Bench, why do agents look superhuman at a 2-hour budget yet fall to half the human score at 32 hours?
options: The 32-hour tasks are drawn from a different, harder task pool than the 2-hour ones
Humans are given reference solutions after 8 hours while agents are not
Agent scores plateau with more time while human scores keep improving, so the budget picks the winner
The scoring normalisation changes from continuous to binary once the budget exceeds 8 hours
questions.explanation: Same seven environments, same scoring; Wijk et al. report agents 4x humans at 2 h, humans narrowly ahead at 8 h and 2x ahead at 32 h because humans show better returns to time.

questions.question: In the time-horizon construction, the 80% horizon equals h50 times 4^(-1/beta). What does this imply about reporting it?
options: The 80% horizon is always exactly one quarter of the 50% horizon regardless of the data
The 80% horizon depends on the fitted slope, so slope assumptions move it far more than they move h50
The 80% horizon is more precisely estimated than h50 because it lies in the dense part of the suite
The 80% horizon can be read directly from the longest solved task without fitting any curve
questions.explanation: A shallow slope pushes h80 far below h50 and a steep one brings them together; METR's Mar 2026 note found reasonable fits change 80% horizons by up to +100% versus -35% for 50% horizons.

questions.question: A suite's longest task is 8 hours and the agent still solves most of the longest tasks. What does the simulator (and METR's note) say about the horizon estimate?
options: Suite-bounded estimators cannot exceed 8 hours and a logistic fit becomes an extrapolation with a much wider interval
The logistic fit remains unbiased and precise because maximum likelihood corrects for the missing long tasks
The horizon should be reported as exactly 8 hours since that is the longest task the agent completed
The estimate is unaffected as long as at least 200 short tasks are present to anchor the curve
questions.explanation: Isotonic and rolling estimators pin to the ceiling (16 h reads 7.2 h in the default run) while the logistic's CI widens from x3.1 to x9.5; METR says the right tail is not meaningfully constrained.

questions.question: METR estimates that 80% of individual human baselines fall within about 3x of a task's true length. Through which mechanism does this noise distort the horizon?
options: It adds the same constant offset to every task time, shifting both horizons up by a fixed factor
It makes bootstrap resampling invalid, so intervals must be computed analytically instead
It only affects tasks shorter than one hour, where repeat baselines are rarely collected
Noise in the x-variable attenuates the fitted slope and rotates the curve about the data centroid, pushing far-side horizons outward
questions.explanation: Classical errors-in-variables: the replicate suites show median slope 0.53 against a true 0.6 and inflated 50% horizons, matching METR's SIMEX estimate of roughly 30% inflation.

questions.question: Claude Opus 4.6's system card reported that the model saturated most automated AI R&D evaluations and the threshold decision leaned on a 16-person staff survey. What is the measurement lesson?
options: Staff surveys are a more accurate instrument than benchmarks and should replace them for all thresholds
A saturated benchmark fails silently, so trend extrapolation through saturated points is unsafe and new long or held-out tasks are needed
Saturation proves the threshold was crossed, so the framework should have triggered its mitigations automatically
Benchmarks saturate only when the judge is an LLM, so human-graded rubrics would have avoided the problem
questions.explanation: The score stops moving while capability keeps moving; the remedies are structural (long tasks, private pools, live tasks), and the survey's split is disputed across secondary sources.
